question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Scottsdale?
body:
## Direct Answer

You find a fractional CRO in Scottsdale through four reliable channels: specialized fractional-executive networks and marketplaces, RevOps and go-to-market consultancies with Arizona benches, warm referrals from your local investor and founder community, and vetted independent operators surfaced on LinkedIn or through Scottsdale business groups. The right path depends on your revenue stage, how many hours a week you actually need, and whether you want a plug-in operator or a strategist who rebuilds your entire commercial engine.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives a growing Scottsdale company senior commercial leadership — sales, marketing alignment, and RevOps — for a fraction of a full-time executive's cost and time commitment. But "where do I find one" is really three questions stacked together: where the supply actually lives, how to tell a real operator from a resume, and how to structure the engagement so the person you hire produces measurable pipeline instead of a slide deck. This guide walks each layer, with the sourcing channels ranked by how they tend to perform for companies in the $2M–$30M range that dominate the Scottsdale and greater Phoenix market.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO and when does a Scottsdale company need one?

A fractional CRO is an experienced revenue leader who works with your company part-time — typically one to three days a week — under a fixed monthly retainer rather than a full-time salary plus equity package. They own the same mandate a full-time CRO would: aligning sales and marketing, building or fixing the sales process, standing up forecasting and pipeline discipline, coaching the sales team or first sales hire, and owning the number the board cares about. The difference is scope of time and cost, not scope of authority. A good fractional CRO walks in with authority delegated by the CEO and treats the engagement as if the outcome is theirs to own.

Scottsdale has become an unusually good market for this model. The metro's economy skews toward founder-led B2B software, fintech, healthtech, and professional-services firms that have crossed the "founder can no longer personally close every deal" threshold but cannot yet justify a $350K–$500K fully-loaded CRO. That gap — too big for the founder to run sales alone, too small for a full C-suite hire — is exactly where fractional leadership fits. If your company has product-market fit, a few reps or account executives, and revenue that has stalled or is growing without any repeatable system behind it, you are the textbook candidate. If you have zero validated customers, you likely need a fractional VP of Sales or a founder-led selling motion first, not a CRO. For a fuller breakdown of the readiness signals, see the diagnostic on [when to hire a fractional revenue leader](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-readiness).

The clearest trigger is a specific, painful gap between where revenue is and where it should be, paired with a leadership team that knows what "good" looks like but has never built it. A fractional CRO closes that gap on a timeline — usually a three-to-twelve-month engagement — and either transitions out or converts to full-time once the engine justifies it.

## Where do fractional CROs actually come from in the Scottsdale and Phoenix market?

The supply of fractional revenue leaders concentrates in a handful of channels, and each one attracts a different type of operator. Ranking them by how consistently they produce a strong hire for a mid-market Scottsdale company:

**Fractional-executive networks and marketplaces** are the fastest way to see vetted supply. Platforms and communities such as Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum, and the Fractional Executives community aggregate operators who have already committed to the fractional model — meaning they are not job-hunting for a full-time role and treating you as a bridge. These networks pre-screen for real operating history, which removes the biggest risk: hiring a career VP who has never actually built a system from scratch. The tradeoff is that marketplace operators are often serving several clients, so you compete for their best hours.

**RevOps and go-to-market consultancies** are the second channel, and often the strongest for companies that want a system rebuilt, not just a leader parked. A consultancy brings a fractional CRO plus a bench — RevOps analysts, a HubSpot or Salesforce admin, a demand-gen resource — so the leader is not the only pair of hands. For a company whose CRM is a mess and whose forecasting is a spreadsheet guess, this bundled model moves faster than a lone operator. The pattern to look for is a firm that leads with diagnosis and hands you an owned system, not one that sells you seats. See our comparison of the [fractional CRO versus RevOps consultancy decision](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-vs-consultancy) for how to choose between a solo operator and a bundled team.

**Warm referrals from the local ecosystem** are the highest-signal but lowest-volume channel. Scottsdale's density of PE-backed and VC-backed companies, plus active groups like the Arizona Technology Council, StartupAZ, and the local chapters of founder and CEO peer networks (Vistage, EO, YPO), means the best fractional operators are usually one or two introductions away. Ask three portfolio-company CEOs or your board who fixed their revenue engine, and the same two or three names tend to recur. A referral comes with a built-in reference and a track record you can verify in a ten-minute call.

**LinkedIn and direct sourcing** round out the list. Searching "fractional CRO" plus "Scottsdale" or "Phoenix" surfaces independents, but the signal-to-noise ratio is the worst of the four channels — the title has become popular enough that many people wearing it are between full-time roles. Use LinkedIn to research and validate operators you found through the other three channels rather than as your primary funnel.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Need a fractional CRO in Scottsdale] --> B{What do you need most}
  B -->|Vetted pre committed operators| C[Fractional networks and marketplaces]
  B -->|System rebuilt with a bench| D[RevOps and GTM consultancy]
  B -->|Highest trust and references| E[Warm referrals from local ecosystem]
  B -->|Research and validation only| F[LinkedIn and direct sourcing]
  C --> G[Shortlist of three candidates]
  D --> G
  E --> G
  F --> G
  G --> H[Structured interview and scorecard]
  H --> I[Paid pilot or first ninety days]
```

The practical move is to run two or three channels in parallel rather than betting on one. Post the need to a marketplace, ask your board and two peer CEOs for referrals, and shortlist one consultancy. Within two weeks you will have a comparable set of three to five candidates.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire an expensive advisor?

The single biggest failure mode is hiring a strategist who produces a beautiful plan and no pipeline. Vetting has to filter for operators who have personally built and run the thing you need built, in a company that looks like yours. Run every candidate through the same scorecard so you are comparing on evidence, not charisma.

Start with **stage and motion fit**. A CRO who scaled a $50M enterprise field-sales org is often the wrong hire for a $4M company selling a $15K product through inbound and inside sales. The motions are different sciences. Ask exactly what revenue band and sales motion they have operated in, and weight recent, hands-on experience over impressive logos from a decade ago. Then probe **specific, ownable outcomes**: not "grew revenue 40%," but "which levers, over what period, and what would your CEO at the time say you personally owned?" Real operators answer with mechanisms — pipeline coverage ratios, win-rate changes, ramp-time reductions — because they lived inside the numbers.

Reference-check like it matters, because it does. Talk to at least two CEOs who hired the candidate as a fractional, and ask the one question that separates operators from advisors: "Did the system they built keep working after they left?" A fractional CRO's job is to install something durable and then get out of the way. If the machine collapsed when they walked, you are hiring a dependency, not a leader. Our guide on [structuring a fractional CRO engagement](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-engagement) covers the contract terms and success metrics that make durability enforceable.

Finally, insist on a **diagnostic before a decision**. A strong candidate will want to look at your pipeline data, your CRM, your recent deals, and your team before quoting a plan or a price. Someone who pitches a generic playbook in the first meeting without asking hard questions about your funnel is selling a template. The best fractional operators run a short paid diagnostic first — a one-to-three-week assessment that produces a prioritized plan — which doubles as a low-risk audition for both sides.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate] --> B{Stage and motion fit}
  B -->|No| X[Pass]
  B -->|Yes| C{Ownable outcomes with mechanisms}
  C -->|Vague| X
  C -->|Specific| D{References confirm durable systems}
  D -->|System collapsed after exit| X
  D -->|System survived| E{Leads with a diagnostic}
  E -->|Sells a template| X
  E -->|Runs an assessment first| F[Move to paid pilot]
```

Treat the first thirty to ninety days as the real interview. A short pilot with a defined deliverable — a rebuilt forecast, a cleaned pipeline, a documented sales process — tells you more than any number of reference calls, and it costs a fraction of a bad annual commitment.

## What should a fractional CRO cost in Scottsdale, and how are engagements structured?

Pricing for fractional executives varies widely by scope, hours, and the operator's track record, so treat any single number with suspicion — the honest answer is that it depends on the model you choose. The three common structures are a **monthly retainer** (a fixed fee for a set number of days per week or per month), a **project or diagnostic fee** (a defined deliverable over a fixed window), and **hybrid arrangements** that pair a retainer with performance-linked upside or equity. Retainers dominate because they align the operator to ongoing ownership rather than a one-time deliverable.

The variables that move the price are the number of days per week, the seniority and track record of the operator, whether a consultancy bundles a supporting bench, and the length of the commitment. A one-day-a-week advisory relationship with a solo operator sits at the low end; a three-day-a-week engagement with a former public-company CRO plus a RevOps analyst sits at the high end. Because the market is unregulated and quotes are bespoke, the right approach is to get comparable proposals from three candidates for the same scope and let the range reveal itself. Ask each to quote the identical deliverable set so you are comparing price against a fixed outcome, not against vague promises.

Whatever the structure, tie payment to a written scope with named success metrics — pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, ramp time, win rate — and a defined review cadence. The engagements that go wrong are almost always the ones that never defined what "done" or "working" meant. A fractional CRO should be comfortable being measured on the number, because owning the number is the entire point of the role. Build in a clean off-ramp too: a month-to-month or quarter-to-quarter term after an initial pilot lets you scale up, scale down, or convert to full-time as the engine matures, without being locked into a bad fit.

## How is a fractional CRO different from a fractional VP of Sales or a sales consultant?

These three roles get conflated constantly, and hiring the wrong one wastes months. A **fractional CRO** owns the full commercial engine — sales, marketing alignment, revenue operations, and the forecast. They operate at the strategy-and-systems altitude, set the go-to-market motion, and hold the CEO's number. A **fractional VP of Sales** owns the sales team specifically: hiring reps, coaching, quota-setting, and pipeline execution. They live closer to the deals. A **sales consultant or trainer** advises and teaches but does not own outcomes or carry a number — they leave you a methodology, not a running system.

The practical rule: hire a fractional CRO when the problem spans sales *and* marketing *and* operations, and no one on the leadership team can see the whole board. Hire a fractional VP of Sales when your go-to-market is sound but your sales team is under-built or under-managed. Hire a consultant when you have leadership in place and need a specific skill injected — a new methodology, a comp-plan redesign, a one-time enablement push. Many Scottsdale founders reach for a CRO when a VP of Sales would have fit the actual gap, paying for strategic breadth they did not need. Diagnose the gap first, then match the role to it — our breakdown of [fractional revenue roles compared](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-revenue-roles) maps each role to the symptoms that call for it.

The other real distinction is durability of impact. A consultant's deliverable is knowledge; a fractional VP's deliverable is a functioning sales team; a fractional CRO's deliverable is a self-sustaining revenue system that keeps producing after they transition out. If what you need is a machine that outlives the engagement, the CRO altitude is the right one — provided you vet for operators who actually build durable systems rather than dependencies.

## What does the first ninety days with a fractional CRO look like?

A strong engagement front-loads diagnosis and sequences quick wins ahead of the deep rebuild, so the CEO sees momentum while the durable system is still being installed. The first two to three weeks are almost entirely assessment: the CRO pulls apart your pipeline data, sits in on live deals, interviews the sales team, audits the CRM and the current forecast, and maps where revenue actually leaks. This is unglamorous and essential — skipping it is how you get a generic playbook applied to a company it does not fit.

By roughly day thirty, a good fractional CRO delivers a prioritized plan with a small number of high-leverage fixes rather than a sprawling transformation. Common early wins are cleaning and re-staging the pipeline so the forecast means something, tightening the qualification criteria so reps stop chasing dead deals, and installing a weekly pipeline review that creates accountability. These produce visible results fast and buy the trust needed for the harder structural work — comp-plan redesign, marketing-and-sales alignment, hiring or replacing reps — that fills days sixty through ninety.

The tell of a good engagement is that by the end of ninety days the company has a repeatable, documented system that the internal team can run, plus a clear read on whether the trajectory justifies converting to a full-time CRO or continuing fractional. The tell of a bad one is ninety days of advice and no operational change. Insist on a scorecard reviewed at thirty, sixty, and ninety days so the relationship is measured on installed systems and pipeline movement, not on activity.

## Related questions

### How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work?
Typically one to three days per week, set by a retainer. Early-stage or single-motion companies often need one to two days; a full engine rebuild across sales, marketing, and RevOps usually justifies three.

### Can a fractional CRO become a full-time CRO?
Yes, and it is a common path. A fractional engagement doubles as an extended mutual audition; if the revenue engine grows to justify a full-time hire and the fit is strong, converting the incumbent is lower-risk than a cold executive search.

### Do fractional CROs work with pre-revenue startups?
Rarely, and usually it is the wrong fit. Pre-revenue companies need founder-led selling or a fractional VP of Sales to find product-market fit first. A CRO adds value once there is a repeatable motion to scale and align.

### Is a fractional CRO worth it for a company under $2M in revenue?
Sometimes, but often a fractional VP of Sales or a RevOps consultant is the better-matched spend. A CRO earns their keep when the problem spans sales, marketing, and operations simultaneously rather than one function.

### How long do fractional CRO engagements last?
Most run three to twelve months, structured month-to-month or quarter-to-quarter after an initial pilot. The goal is to install a durable system and then transition out or convert to full-time, not to create a permanent dependency.

## FAQ

**How do I find a fractional CRO specifically in Scottsdale rather than remote?**
Lead with local channels: the Arizona Technology Council, StartupAZ, and CEO peer networks like Vistage, EO, and YPO concentrate operators who know the Scottsdale and Phoenix market. Many strong fractional CROs work partly remote, so weigh local presence against fit — a great operator two days a week beats a mediocre one down the street.

**What's the difference between a fractional CRO and an interim CRO?**
An interim CRO is a full-time, temporary placeholder filling a vacancy until a permanent hire is found. A fractional CRO is a permanent part-time arrangement — they are intentionally not full-time and often serve several companies. Interim is about bridging a gap in headcount; fractional is about right-sizing senior leadership to what a growing company can use.

**Should I hire a solo fractional CRO or a consultancy?**
Choose a solo operator when you need a leader to own strategy and your internal team can execute. Choose a consultancy when your systems need a rebuild and you lack the hands to do it — the bundled RevOps bench moves faster. Match the model to whether your gap is leadership or execution capacity.

**How do I know if a fractional CRO candidate is actually experienced?**
Ask for specific ownable outcomes with mechanisms — win-rate changes, pipeline coverage, ramp-time reductions — not vague growth percentages. Reference-check whether the systems they built survived after they left. Insist they run a diagnostic before quoting a plan. Operators answer with numbers; advisors answer with frameworks.

**What should I prepare before bringing in a fractional CRO?**
Give them access to your CRM, pipeline data, recent closed and lost deals, current forecast, comp plans, and the sales team for interviews. The faster they can diagnose reality, the faster they deliver value. Clean data is not required — they will assess its state as part of the audit.

**Can a fractional CRO fix a broken CRM and RevOps stack?**
A fractional CRO owns the strategy and will diagnose the problems, but repairing a broken Salesforce or HubSpot instance usually needs a RevOps analyst or admin alongside them. If your stack is the core issue, favor a consultancy with a bench or pair a solo CRO with dedicated RevOps support.

**How is success measured in a fractional CRO engagement?**
Through a written scorecard tied to named metrics — pipeline coverage ratio, forecast accuracy, win rate, sales-cycle length, and ramp time — reviewed at thirty, sixty, and ninety days. The engagement should also produce a documented, repeatable system your internal team can run without the CRO present.

**What happens when the fractional CRO engagement ends?**
A well-run engagement ends with a durable system handed off to your internal team, a clear read on whether to hire full-time, and no operational collapse when the operator steps back. Many relationships transition to a lighter advisory retainer or convert to full-time rather than ending cleanly.
